# Esophagectomy Techniques

**Katherine D. Gray & Daniela Molena**

*Chapter 33 — Surgical Therapy for Esophageal Cancer*

---

## Introduction

- Surgical resection is the cornerstone for early/locally advanced esophageal cancer without systemic metastases
- Multimodality therapy offers the highest likelihood of cure for locoregional disease
- Management should be individualized via multidisciplinary panels
- Key factors: physiologic status, tumor type/location, stage of disease

::: {.notes}
Surgery is the cornerstone, but must be individualized via multidisciplinary panels based on patient status, tumor type, location, and stage.
:::

---

## Operative Variables

| Variable | Options |
|----------|---------|
| Fields explored | Abdomen, chest, neck (1, 2, or 3 fields) |
| Anastomosis location | Thoracic vs. cervical |
| Approach | Open, thoracoscopic/laparoscopic, robotic, hybrid |

- Exact approach depends on **tumor location** and **surgeon/institutional preference**

---

## Preoperative Patient Assessment

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**History & Physical Focus**
- Barrett's esophagus, GERD, achalasia
- Prior surgeries, functional status
- Cardiac and respiratory comorbidities
- Smoking cessation & alcohol use

**Workup**
- Comprehensive bloodwork, ECG, PFTs
- Nutritional optimization (feeding tube if needed)
- Prehabilitation program when available
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Risk Factors by Histology**

| Adenocarcinoma | Squamous Cell |
|----------------|---------------|
| Increased age | Alcohol use |
| Obesity | Tobacco use |
| Tobacco use | Cirrhosis |
| Reflux disease | |

- Advanced age alone is **not** a contraindication
:::
:::

---

## Oncologic Workup for Resectability

**Candidates:** Early (T1b-2N0) or locoregional (T2-4aN0-3) disease

- **Endoscopy ± EUS:** Limited utility for earliest stages or bulky tumors
- **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis:** Vasculature, morphology, extent
- **PET-CT:** Metastatic evaluation (note: signet cell tumors may be silent)
- **Brain imaging:** If neurologic symptoms
- **Bronchoscopy:** For proximal/mid-esophageal tumors (rule out airway invasion)
- **Staging laparoscopy:** Signet cell cancers or tumors extending &gt;3 cm into stomach

---

## Multimodality Therapy & Timing

- Most resectable patients best treated with multimodality therapy
- Common regimens:
  - Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (**CROSS protocol**)
  - Perioperative chemotherapy
- **Nivolumab** approved in adjuvant setting for residual disease after neoadjuvant CRT + surgery
- Restaging PET-CT after induction
- Surgery scheduled **5–8 weeks** after chemoradiation completion

---

## Extent of Resection: Three Main Considerations

1. **Tumor location**
2. **Obtaining sufficient margin**
3. **Extent of lymphadenectomy**

**Margins**
- Proximal: **12 cm** when possible
- Distal: **5 cm** optimal
- Circumferential: Negative margin ≥ **1 mm** favorable

---

## Main Resection Techniques

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Ivor Lewis**
- Two-field resection
- Intrathoracic anastomosis
- Preferred for middle-distal/esophagogastric tumors

**McKeown**
- Three-field resection
- Cervical anastomosis
- Required for high/high-middle tumors

**Transhiatal**
- Avoids thoracotomy
- Limited lymphadenectomy
- Best for intramucosal tumors, dysplasia, or benign disease
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Vagal-Sparing Esophagectomy (VSE)**
- Variant of transhiatal
- Non-oncologic or very early intramucosal cancers
- Preserves vagus nerves → better functional outcomes
:::
:::

---

## Lymphadenectomy Requirements

- Lymphatic dissemination occurs early and unpredictably
- Once tumor penetrates submucosa, up to **50%** have nodal metastases
- **≥18 lymph nodes** needed for accurate staging and survival benefit
- **En bloc esophagectomy:** Resection with pleural surfaces, pericardium, posterior lymphatic tissue, azygos arch, and thoracic duct
- Many centers now use **modified en bloc** preserving adjacent structures

---

## Minimally Invasive vs. Open Esophagectomy

**Historical Context**
- First MIE reports: Cuschieri (1992, thoracoscopic) and DePaula (1995, laparoscopic transhiatal)
- Popularized by Luketich (University of Pittsburgh, ~2000)

**Current Practice**
- &gt;50% of esophagectomies performed minimally invasively at reporting institutions

**Key Benefit**
- Reduction in respiratory complications
  - TIME trial: 34% → 12% pulmonary complications
  - MIRO trial: similar reduction with hybrid approach

---

## MIE: Thoracoscopic/Laparoscopic Approach

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Advantages**
- Reduced postoperative pain
- Faster recovery
- Decreased wound infection
- Less blood loss
- Shorter hospital stay

**Prerequisites**
- Advanced minimally invasive equipment
- Significant surgeon skill & learning curve (35–40 cases)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Relative Challenges**
- Extensive adhesions
- Tumor extension into adjacent structures (lack of tactile feedback)
- Single-lung ventilation preferred but not always necessary
:::
:::

---

## Robotic Esophagectomy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Advantages**
- 3D optics
- Improved dexterity & ergonomics
- Surgeon controls camera/retraction
- Built-in near-infrared fluorescence (ICG) for conduit perfusion

**Disadvantages**
- Cost & complexity
- Personnel issues, room layout, docking
- Learning curve surmountable with formal training
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Outcomes**
- Long-term oncologic outcomes expected comparable to non-robotic MIE
- ROBOT trial: fewer overall/pulmonary complications vs. open, lower pain scores, improved QoL
:::
:::

---

## Open Ivor Lewis: Abdominal Phase

1. Midline laparotomy; inspect peritoneal cavity & liver
2. Mobilize liver segments 2/3 (divide left triangular ligament)
3. Incise pars flaccida; identify right gastric artery
4. Divide gastrocolic omentum, **preserve gastroepiploic arcade**
5. Divide short gastric vessels close to spleen
6. Remove lymph node tissue over hepatic artery, portal vein, celiac axis
7. Ligate coronary vein; divide left gastric artery at origin
8. Kocher maneuver if needed
9. Tubularize stomach with linear stapler (≥5 cm from tumor distally)
10. Oversew staple line; pyloric procedure optional; place feeding jejunostomy

---

## Open Ivor Lewis: Thoracic Phase

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Position & Access**
- Left lateral decubitus
- Right posterolateral thoracotomy (5th or 6th intercostal space)
- Divide inferior pulmonary ligament

**Key Steps**
- Divide pleura over right main bronchus (avoid thermal injury)
- Ligate/close azygos arch with stapler
- Preserve pleural cranial to azygos as pedicled flap for anastomosis
- Remove right paratracheal nodes
- Divide right vagal nerve & bronchial artery
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Dissection**
- Incise pleura over vertebral bodies; divide intercostal veins
- Follow intercostal arteries to aortic adventitial plane
- Ligate direct aortic branches to esophagus
- Ligate communicating veins to hemiazygos
- Identify & transect thoracic duct (place heavy nonresorbable ligature caudally)
- Dissect anteriorly along pericardium; remove subcarinal nodes en bloc
- Divide left vagus at left main bronchus
:::
:::

---

## Open Ivor Lewis: Anastomosis

- Divide esophagus above azygos arch
- Deliver gastric tube through hiatus (prevent rotation)
- Place purse-string Prolene 1.0 suture
- Estimate diameter with 30-mL balloon catheter
- Place anvil; create end-to-side anastomosis with **25-mm or 29-mm circular stapler**
- Close gastrotomy with linear stapler; oversew
- Pass nasogastric tube into distal stomach
- Wrap omental tissue around anastomosis

---

## Open McKeown Esophagectomy

**Three-hole approach**

1. **Thoracic phase first:** Transthoracic mobilization as far into neck as possible
2. **Abdominal phase:** Midline laparotomy, gastric mobilization, lymphadenectomy, conduit creation (same as Ivor Lewis)
3. **Cervical phase:**
   - Left neck incision along sternocleidomastoid border
   - Divide omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid
   - Ligate middle thyroid vein & inferior thyroid artery
   - Dissect to prevertebral fascia; reach thoracic inlet plane
   - Create plane between esophagus and trachea
   - Deliver esophagus to neck; divide at thoracic inlet

---

## McKeown: Conduit Delivery & Anastomosis

- Suture umbilical tape to proximal specimen end
- Remove specimen transabdominally; tape passes through mediastinum
- Reaffix tape to gastric conduit top
- Wrap conduit in plastic bag for atraumatic passage
- Pass via posterior mediastinum to neck (avoid tension/torsion)
- **End-to-end anastomosis (EEA)** with single-layer running suture
- Place nonabsorbable hiatus sutures to prevent visceral herniation
- Pass nasogastric tube; place jejunal feeding tube

---

## Open Transhiatal Esophagectomy (THE)

**Indications**
- Intramucosal tumors, dysplasia, or benign disease
- **Contraindicated** if suspected mediastinal invasion

**Technique**
1. Abdominal lymphadenectomy & gastric mobilization
2. Incise hiatus anteriorly or circumferentially (ligate diaphragmatic vein)
3. En bloc dissection of lower thoracic esophagus under direct vision (up to inferior pulmonary veins)
4. Avoid dissection at right side of aorta (protect thoracic duct)
5. Create gastric tube
6. Expose cervical esophagus (as in McKeown)
7. Complete blunt dissection from above and below
8. Divide esophagus in neck; remove specimen from abdomen
9. Pass Foley catheter through mediastinum; deliver conduit; cervical anastomosis

---

## Vagal-Sparing Esophagectomy (VSE)

**Concept**
- Modification of THE for non-oncologic, high-grade dysplasia, or very early intramucosal cancer
- Maximizes functional outcomes at expense of lymphadenectomy
- **Contraindicated** for submucosal tumors (risk of nodal metastases)

**Benefits of Vagal Preservation**
- Minimizes dumping, diarrhea
- Reduces early satiety and reflux (depending on reconstruction)
- Preserves left gastric arterial trunk & pyloric branches → excellent graft perfusion
- **No pyloroplasty needed**

---

## VSE Technique

1. Open hiatus; encircle anterior & posterior vagal trunks with vessel loop
2. Retract vagi gently to patient's right
3. Dissect gastroesophageal fat pad from left side, bringing anterior vagus to right of esophagus
4. Perform **highly selective vagotomy** above crow's foot near antrum
5. Skeletonize lesser curve up to distal esophagus; separate vagal trunks from esophagus
6. Mobilize greater curve (standard fashion)
7. Neck exposure; Penrose drain around esophagus
8. Bluntly free upper mediastinal esophagus
9. Gastrotomy near GEJ (or staple cardia with small opening)
10. Pass vein stripper retrograde up esophagus; exit anterior cervical wall
11. Ligate esophagus distal to stripper exit; divide cervical esophagus at exit site
12. Change to large stripper head; invert esophagus on itself (like removing a sock inside-out)
13. Dilate mediastinal tract with 90cc Foley balloon (2–3 passes)
14. Pull up gastric tube; standard anastomosis; suture to crura

---

## Minimally Invasive Ivor Lewis: Abdominal Phase

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Setup**
- Supine, footboard, steep reverse Trendelenburg
- Double-lumen tube for thoracic phase
- 5 abdominal ports + Nathanson liver retractor
- Esophagogastroduodenoscopy first to evaluate tumor & stomach
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Key Steps**
- Inspect for metastases
- Open gastrohepatic ligament; expose celiac trunk branches
- Complete lymphadenectomy (hepatic, left gastric, splenic arteries)
- Divide left gastric vessels with vascular stapler
- Mobilize greater curvature (preserve gastroepiploic arcade)
- Divide short gastrics & phrenoesophageal attachments
- Mobilize right gastroepiploic pedicle to base
- Transhiatal dissection of distal esophagus; Penrose drain left in mediastinum
:::
:::

---

## MIE Abdominal Phase: Conduit & Ports

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Figure 33.1**  
*Abdominal MIE port placement*  
- 5 ports + Nathanson retractor
- Skilled assistant essential
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Figure 33.2**  
*Complete abdominal lymphadenectomy*  
- Skeletonize hepatic, splenic, left gastric arteries
- Divide left gastric vessels at base with endoscopic stapler

**Conduit Creation**
- 5-cm wide gastric tube with linear stapler
- Start below incisura for complete unfurling
- Leave undivided at fundus to facilitate retrieval
- 14 French feeding jejunostomy percutaneously
:::
:::

---

## Minimally Invasive Ivor Lewis: Thoracic Phase

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Setup**
- Left lateral decubitus; right lung collapsed
- 4 trocars + CO₂ insufflation (8 mmHg)
- Alternative: prone positioning (no lung collapse needed)

**Dissection**
- Divide pulmonary ligament to inferior pulmonary vein
- Open posterior mediastinal pleura from hiatus to azygos
- Divide azygos with vascular stapler
- Retrieve Penrose drain for retraction
- En bloc dissection from pericardium, aorta, airways, contralateral pleura
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Division & Lymphadenectomy**
- Divide esophagus at thoracic inlet with stapler
- Send proximal margin for frozen section
- Complete subcarinal lymphadenectomy
- Extend to paratracheal nodes for SCC or mid-esophageal tumors (consider cervical anastomosis)

**Conduit Retrieval**
- Pull conduit into chest; divide from stomach with linear stapler
- Ensure proper orientation (avoid twisting)
- Extend inferomedial port to ~3 cm with wound protector
- Remove specimen in bag; introduce circular stapler
:::
:::

## MIE Anastomosis: Transoral Circular Stapler

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Preferred Approach**
1. Orogastric tube connected to anvil inserted through mouth to esophageal stump
2. Create small opening next to staple line
3. Pull tube until anvil passes through mouth into esophageal stump
4. Position visibly within esophagotomy; disconnect tubing
5. Evaluate conduit perfusion with **ICG fluorescence imaging**
6. Introduce EEA stapler through enlarged chest incision into gastrotomy at conduit tip
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Completion**
- Pull conduit over stapler; piston exits at greater curvature
- Engage anvil & stapler; fire
- Typically use **25-mm anvil** with **green stapler (4.8 mm)**
- Resect excess gastric tip with linear stapler (≥1 cm from anastomosis)
- Position greater fat pad between conduit and airways
- Secure conduit to right diaphragm with interrupted suture
:::
:::

---

## MIE Anastomosis: Other Techniques

**Transthoracic Circular**
- Place 25- or 28-mm anvil into esophageal stump from field
- Purse-string closure; complete as above

**Intrathoracic Side-to-Side (Linear Stapler)**
- Align proximal esophagus anterior to stomach
- Stapler through gastrotomy 5–6 cm from conduit top
- Close common enterotomy with linear stapler or sutures

**Figure 33.6**  
*Orvil engaged with circular mechanical stapler to complete anastomosis along greater curvature*

---

## Minimally Invasive McKeown Esophagectomy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Indications**
- Transitioning from open to MIE (avoids intrathoracic anastomosis)
- Cervical/upper thoracic cancers
- Long-segment Barrett's esophagus
- Multifocal disease requiring total thoracic esophagectomy

**Technique**
- Thoracoscopic mobilization
- Laparoscopic conduit creation
- Complete division in abdomen
- Left neck incision (protect recurrent laryngeal nerve)
- Divide cervical esophagus
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Conduit Delivery**
- Pass 22 French Foley catheter from neck to abdomen via posterior mediastinum
- Secure gastric conduit to catheter using sterile ultrasound bag with suction
- Withdraw catheter to deliver conduit to neck

**Anastomosis**
- Two-layer handsewn EEA
:::
:::

---

## Minimally Invasive Transhiatal Esophagectomy

1. Laparoscopic abdominal lymphadenectomy & conduit construction
2. Transhiatal dissection under direct visualization (enlarge hiatus at right crus)
3. Continue mobilization to level of carina
4. Left cervical incision; divide proximal esophagus
5. Suture Penrose to proximal distal esophagus
6. Deliver esophagus into abdomen (pulls Penrose through mediastinum)
7. Remove specimen via abdomen
8. Suture Penrose to gastric conduit; deliver to neck
9. Standard cervical anastomosis

**Advantage:** Superior mediastinal visualization vs. open THE; decreased blood loss, fewer respiratory complications, shorter stay

---

## Laparoscopic Hand-Assisted Esophagectomy

- **Hand access device (Lap Disc)** in 7-cm midline incision
- Surgeon uses laparoscopic instruments + hand assistance
- Tactile sensation facilitates gentle manipulation and blunt dissection
- Quicker operation
- Lower complication rate & short recovery
- Useful adjunctive training tool for MIE transition

---

## Robotic Ivor Lewis: Abdominal Phase

**Figure 33.9**  
*Port placement for abdominal phase of robotic esophagectomy*

- Camera: 18 cm inferior to xiphoid
- Single left robotic arm; two right robotic arms
- Ports ≤2–3 cm superior to camera port
- 9 cm apart (Si system) or 8 cm (Xi system)
- 5-mm liver retractor port; 12-mm assistant port (right lower quadrant)

---

## Robotic Abdominal Dissection

**Instruments**
- Left arm: Cadiere forceps
- Right arm: Vessel Sealer
- Second right arm: Thoracic grasper (Si) or tip-up fenestrated grasper (Xi)

**Steps**
1. Divide greater omentum from greater curvature (preserve gastroepiploic vessels)
2. Divide short gastric vessels; preserve omental flap for anastomosis
3. Clear left side of hiatus from top down under esophagus
4. Enter lesser sac through lesser omentum
5. Test clamp replaced left hepatic artery (up to 12% of patients); preserve if liver ischemic
6. Circumferential dissection around esophagus at hiatus (avoid left pleura)
7. Place Penrose drain; divide left gastric pedicle after test clamp
8. Pyloromyotomy/plasty optional (authors generally omit)
9. Create conduit with stapler (4-mm height, 45–60 mm length)
10. Place jejunostomy (often laparoscopically after undocking)

---

## Robotic Ivor Lewis: Thoracic Phase

**Figure 33.10**  
*Patient positioning and port placement for thoracic phase*

- Nearly prone position; keep right arm/shoulder low
- Right robotic arm: axilla (8 mm; 12 mm if robotic stapling)
- Camera: 9 cm from right arm (8 mm Xi; 12 mm Si)
- Left robotic arm: 9 cm from camera (12 mm Xi if robotic stapling)
- Second left arm: posterior to midaxillary line above diaphragm
- Assistant port: triangulated behind left arm and camera

---

## Robotic Thoracic Dissection & Anastomosis

**Dissection**
- Retract lung anteriorly; divide inferior pulmonary ligament
- Resect stations 8, 9, then 7 (expose carina & mainstem bronchi)
- Divide azygos with vascular stapler (fire as posteriorly as possible)
- Dissect esophagus proximally to thoracic inlet; posteriorly off aorta (avoid thoracic duct)
- Grasp Penrose drain; retract for dissection
- Avoid left pleural space unless resecting gross disease

**Advantage:** Much of distal neck dissection possible via chest → may decrease recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

---

## Robotic Anastomosis Options

**Handsewn**
- Wristed instruments make this feasible
- Outer layer: 3-0 silk; Inner layer: 3-0 absorbable
- Anterior wall: interrupted 3-0 absorbable + Lembert 3-0 silk

**Side-to-Side (Linear Stapler)**
- 20–30 mm common channel
- Close common channel with second stapler fire or two-layer handsewn closure

**Circular Stapler**
- Purse-string in esophagus; anvil placed
- Gastrotomy at conduit tip; stapler positioned posteriorly
- Caution: avoid aortic injury when extending tip
- Inspect anastomosis; endoscopic leak test optional

---

## Robotic McKeown Esophagectomy

- Robotic intrathoracic mobilization + robotic gastric conduit
- Complete division of specimen in abdomen
- Extensive robotic periesophageal dissection into thoracic inlet
- Place Penrose in chest; staple/tie ends; push into superior mediastinum
- Left neck incision; use Penrose to pull esophagus into incision
- Pull specimen and conduit gently up through chest
- Keep camera in abdomen during passage to prevent twisting
- Divide esophagus sharply; staple specimen off conduit
- Posterior wall: 3.5–4.5 mm stapler; anterior wall: interrupted silk + stapler
- Optional Lembert buttressing layer

---

## Conduit Size & Functional Outcome

**Common Functional Impairments**
- Reflux (~40%)
- Delayed gastric emptying (~40%)
- Dumping syndrome (~20%)

**Counseling**
- Frequent small meals
- Elevated head of bed
- Proton pump inhibitors

**Technical Modifications**
- **Tubularization** (rather than whole stomach) reduces delayed emptying and reflux
- Allows longer conduit for high anastomoses
- **Width ~5 cm** favored (too narrow &lt;4 cm increases ischemia/leak risk)

---

## Pyloric Emptying Procedure

- Options: pyloromyotomy, pyloroplasty, intrapyloric Botulinum toxin
- Meta-analysis shows **no reduction** in delayed gastric emptying impact
- May predispose to dumping syndrome and unnecessary complications
- **Authors do not routinely perform** pyloric drainage

---

## Assessment of Conduit Perfusion

**Traditional**
- Visual inspection & palpation of right gastroepiploic pedicle

**ICG Fluorescence Angiography**
- Intravenous ICG + near-infrared camera
- Particularly convenient with robotic platform (built-in)
- Meta-analysis: reduces anastomotic leak and graft necrosis
- **90-second perfusion** proposed as quantitative cutoff

**Preconditioning**
- Divide short gastric arteries; clip/staple left gastric pedicle preoperatively
- Promotes neovascularization via right gastroepiploic pedicle
- Associated with decreased stricture and anastomotic complications

---

## Routine Feeding Jejunostomy

- Authors' practice: routine placement
- Preoperatively if dysphagia/malnutrition present; intraoperatively for all others
- Allows nutritional support during recovery
- Protects patient if anastomotic compromise occurs
- Shown to decrease **30-day all-cause mortality**
- Meticulous technique required (risks: infection, volvulus, obstruction)

---

## Paraconduit Hernia

- **Incidence:** ~10%
- More common after MIE than open
- More common in young patients and those **not** receiving neoadjuvant therapy
- Mechanism: minimal adhesions after MIE; greater hiatal retraction/attenuation

**Prevention**
- Avoid entering left pleura
- Suture conduit to thoracic diaphragmatic hiatus
- Minimize hiatal disruption
- Close hiatus in patients with hiatal hernia

**Repair:** Typically laparoscopic if necessary

---

## Surgical Outcomes: Complications

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Overall Statistics**
- Complication rate: **59%**
- Pneumonia: **14.6%**
- Atrial dysrhythmias: **14.5%**
- Anastomotic leak: **11.4%**
- 30-day mortality: **2.4%**
- 90-day mortality: **4.5%**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Pulmonary Complications**
- Minimized by early ambulation & pain control
- Semi-upright positioning
- Functioning nasogastric tube
- Bronchoscopy for retained secretions

**Cardiac Complications**
- ~17% after open esophagectomy
- Atrial fibrillation majority
- Fluid shifts & systemic inflammatory response
- May indicate anastomotic dehiscence or chest tube irritation
:::
:::

---

## Anastomotic Leak

**Most feared complication** — substantial morbidity/mortality if not salvaged

**Cervical vs. Thoracic**
- Cervical more common (longer conduit, potential pedicle compression, tension)
- Cervical leaks often minimal morbidity (wound opening/drainage + antibiotics)
- Intrathoracic leaks harder to control; may cause empyema/mediastinitis

**Management (Intrathoracic)**
- NPO, hydration, antibiotics
- Pleural/mediastinal drainage (source control)
- Intraluminal covered stents or endoluminal negative pressure devices
- Conduit resection & diversion if fails or conduit ischemia/tracheoesophageal fistula present

---

## MIE Surgical Outcomes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Benefits**
- Minimizes postoperative pain
- Faster recovery
- Decreased wound infection
- Reduced cardiopulmonary complications
- Less blood loss
- Shorter hospital stay

**Immune/Stress Response**
- Improved leukocyte counts
- Lower IL-8 levels
- Reduced stress response
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Meta-Analysis (15,790 esophagectomies)**
- MIE: higher operative time
- MIE: significantly shorter hospital stay, lower mortality, lower overall morbidity
- Advantage driven by pulmonary & cardiovascular complications
- GI complications, leak rate, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury: **similar**

**TIME Trial (RCT)**
- Decreased respiratory complications
- Shorter LOS
- Improved short-term QoL
- 1-year follow-up: similar late complications, improved 1-year QoL
:::
:::

---

## Robotic MIE Outcomes

- Perioperative morbidity & postoperative parameters **similar** to non-robotic MIE
- Retrospective comparisons: similar operative times, blood loss, lymph nodes harvested, LOS, complications
- Operative times comparable; significant speed improvement after first 20 cases
- **ROBOT trial (RCT):** Robotic MIE vs. open
  - Fewer overall & pulmonary complications
  - Lower postoperative pain
  - Improved quality of life

---

## Oncologic Outcomes

**Prognostic Factors**
- Age, gender, weight loss
- Histologic subtype
- Depth of invasion
- Radicality of resection
- Number of involved lymph nodes

**Modern Multimodality Series**
- Median survival after CRT + surgery:
  - SCC: **84 months**
  - Adenocarcinoma: **43 months**

**MIE vs. Open**
- Retrospective studies show **oncologic equivalence**
- Some reports of **higher lymph node harvest** with MIE (magnified visualization)
- R0 resection rates comparable
- TIME trial 3-year follow-up: disease-free survival 36% (open) vs. 40% (MIE)

---

## Unique Circumstances: Salvage Esophagectomy

- Definitive chemoradiotherapy used for proximal SCC or unfit patients
- High locoregional recurrence/persistence rates (up to **51%**)
- Salvage esophagectomy technically demanding
- Centralization of care, improved selection, and familiarity with irradiated fields have decreased morbidity/mortality
- Propensity-matched analysis: in-hospital mortality **not different** from primary surgery after induction CRT
- Higher rates of anastomotic leak and wound complications
- Comparable 3-year overall and disease-free survival

---

## Esophagectomy for Benign Disease

**Indications**
- Obstruction (caustic ingestion, reflux disease)
- Unsalvageable perforation
- Dysmotility (end-stage achalasia, scleroderma)

**Considerations**
- Often technically challenging (fibrosis, reoperative field)
- Long-term functional outcomes are good

**Approach Selection**
- Nonreoperative: transhiatal or vagal-sparing appropriate
- Significant contamination/fibrosis: retrosternal conduit; nongastric conduits may be required
- Individualized based on prior operations, imaging, endoscopy, barium swallow

---

## Summary

- Tailored approach to esophageal cancer management now achieves ~**50% 5-year survival**
- Surgical technique varies by **tumor location** and **institutional experience**
- **Minimally invasive techniques** are increasingly common
- Key technical principles:
  - Adequate margins (12 cm proximal, 5 cm distal)
  - Extensive lymphadenectomy (≥18 nodes)
  - Conduit perfusion assessment (ICG)
  - Careful anastomotic technique
  - Nutritional support (routine jejunostomy)
